sources.title: Human History Map, historical-basemap civilization index
sources.note: Exact repository record for yuezhi: Yuezhi, circa 200 to 100 BCE. The adjacent kushan-empire record begins at the atlas seam in 100 BCE.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-300 BCE historical basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded predecessor snapshot has no exact yuezhi feature. Tested Central Asian and Gansu points do not establish a predecessor identity.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-200 BCE historical basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded exact target feature is one 26-position polygon. It includes Dunhuang and central Hexi test points but excludes tested Ili, Ferghana, Sogdian and Bactrian places.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-100 BCE historical basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded handoff snapshot has no yuezhi feature and instead draws a very large kushan-empire polygon across Bactria, Central Asia and the northwest subcontinent.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1 BCE historical basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded snapshot has neither an exact yuezhi feature nor a kushan-empire feature, exposing an atlas gap rather than a documented political collapse.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-100 CE historical basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded snapshot restores kushan-empire in a smaller Central Asian polygon and assigns another Kushan-labeled feature farther south and west.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Kushan Dynasty I: Dynastic History
sources.note: Lines 41 to 67 trace Yuezhi presence near Gansu, Xiongnu defeats, westward migration, five Bactrian chiefs and Kujula Kadphises becoming king more than a century later.

sources.title: University of Washington Silk Road Seattle, The Han Histories
sources.note: Lines 136 to 166 translate Zhang Qian’s mission and report: migration, a royal succession variant, mobile herding, the Oxus court, Bactrian towns, markets and refusal of alliance.

sources.title: Chinese Text Project, Shiji 123: Account of Dayuan
sources.note: Digital primary text of Shiji chapter 123 preserves the Classical Chinese account and the external Han-era name 大月氏 for the Great Yuezhi.

sources.title: National Institute of Informatics and Toyo Bunko, Shiji volume 123
sources.note: Digitized rare-book witness with DOI metadata identifies chapter 123 as the account of Zhang Qian’s mission to the Dayuezhi and later western diplomacy.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Chinese Turkestan II: In Pre-Islamic Times
sources.note: The early-history section follows Zhang Qian from 138 to 126 BCE, Yuezhi settlement west of Ferghana and the later five Bactrian kingdoms.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bactria I: Pre-Islamic Period
sources.note: Lines 54 to 58 describe Yuezhi camps north of the Oxus, Bactrian petty principalities, five xihou, conflicting western names and Kujula’s later consolidation.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Heliocles I
sources.note: Lines 37 to 40 set out a two-stage Yuezhi advance, the 138 to 126 BCE Zhang Qian mission and posthumous imitations of Greek royal coin types.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Sakas in Afghanistan
sources.note: Lines 33 to 37 distinguish Saka and Yuezhi movements and explain why proposed ethnic assignments of nomadic pottery at Ai Khanum remain hypothetical.

sources.title: J. P. Mallory, The Problem of Tocharian Origins: An Archaeological Perspective
sources.note: Pages 28 to 32 warn that identifying Yuezhi with Tocharian speakers does not provide a secure archaeological or linguistic starting point without separate demonstration.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Khalchayan
sources.note: Lines 33 to 39 describe excavation, disputed dating, palace setting, painted clay sculptures, rulers, aristocrats, deities and a possible dynastic ancestor.

sources.title: Museum of Prehistory and Early History Berlin, Archaeological Treasures from Uzbekistan exhibition texts
sources.note: PDF pages 32 to 33 describe Khalchayan’s portico, throne room, surrounding rooms, royal-family scenes, warrior elite, ceremonies, musicians, masks and comedians.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Greece VIII: Greek Art in Central Asia, Afghanistan and Northwest India
sources.note: Lines 54 to 58 explain how Khalchayan artists used Hellenized sculptural techniques for Iranian royal, battle and equestrian themes.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Dalverzin Tepe
sources.note: Lines 35 to 38 describe first-century BCE growth, a proposed Yuezhi capital identification and the later Kushan town’s walls, zones and mud-brick construction.

sources.title: UNESCO History of Civilizations of Central Asia, City Life in the Kushan Period
sources.note: Pages 291 to 300 survey expanding urban networks, citadels, residential and workshop suburbs, temples and excavated Kushan-period cities across Central Asia.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Afghanistan: Hidden Treasures
sources.note: Tillya Tepe section describes first-century CE nomadic burials, a chieftain and women, gold objects, uncertain causes of death and mixed cultural influences.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Afghanistan: Hidden Treasures photo gallery
sources.note: Object captions document sewn gold appliques, imported stones, dragon motifs, local Bactrian goldsmithing and objects blending steppe, Greek, Indian and Chinese imagery.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Clothing V: In Pre-Islamic Eastern Iran
sources.note: Lines 51 to 53 reconstruct elite clothing shown at Khalchayan: belted mantles, shirts, trousers or leggings, boots, layered dresses, crowns and shoulder cloths.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Central Asia X: Economy Before the Timurids
sources.note: Lines 63 to 68 separate mobile Yuezhi from settled agriculture and describe later Kushan canal irrigation, ploughs, markets, workshops and long-distance commerce.

sources.title: UNESCO History of Civilizations of Central Asia, Economy and Social System in Central Asia in the Kushan Age
sources.note: Crop-raising section lists excavated millet, barley, wheat, fruits, grapes, melons, fodder, sesame and cotton, with clear Kushan-period rather than early Yuezhi scope.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Archaeology V: Pre-Islamic Central Asia
sources.note: Lines 100 to 102 describe gradual first-century CE Kushan consolidation and the local, Hellenistic, Indian and nomadic strands visible in Bactrian material culture.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Kushan Empire
sources.note: The museum chronology connects the Guishang branch to the Yuezhi, places arrival in Bactria around 135 BCE and associates Kujula Kadphises with later unification.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Kingship V: In Eastern Iranian Lands
sources.note: Lines 61 to 67 analyze Kujula’s Greek coin titles, later Bactrian language, mixed divine images and the royal legitimacy program of Kushan inscriptions.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Kushan Dynasty IV: Coinage of the Kushans
sources.note: Coinage study connects Kujula’s campaigns to the five Yuezhi chiefs and explains rulers, languages, scripts, denominations and iconography on Kushan issues.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Kushan Dynasty II: Inscriptions of the Kushans
sources.note: Lines 37 to 61 cover Rabatak, the royal genealogy, Bactrian, Brahmi and Kharosthi records, and a circa 89 CE health wish without recording a treatment.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Kadphises, Vima
sources.note: The epigraphy section gives the Bactrian titulature OOHMO KAΔΦIΣHΣO ϷAO, identifies Vima in the Rabatak genealogy and dates a separate Khalatse record around 112 CE.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, Rabatak Inscription
sources.note: Museum record identifies the 23-line limestone inscription as Bactrian written in Greek script and summarizes its praise of Kushan king Kanishka.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bactrian Language
sources.note: The writing section documents Bactrian seals and monumental inscriptions in Greek-derived script, especially Surkh Kotal, without claiming Bactrian was the original Yuezhi language.

sources.title: British Museum collection, coin of Kanishka I
sources.note: Museum object record identifies a Kanishka I coin with a Bactrian inscription, providing a concrete successor-period witness to language on portable money.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Chinese-Iranian Relations I: In Pre-Islamic Times
sources.note: The opening section connects Zhang Qian’s Yuezhi mission to late second-century BCE contact and distinguishes evidence from unsubstantiated theories of earlier influence.

sources.title: British Academy, The Excavations at Surkh Kotal and the Problem of Hellenism in Bactria and India
sources.note: The excavation report and inscription discussion describe Kushan-period water works, a failing supply and construction or restoration associated with the sanctuary well.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Central Asia III: In Pre-Islamic Times
sources.note: The Hellenistic and post-Hellenistic section states that Yuezhi established power north of the Oxus and that one branch expanded south as the Kushan empire in the first century CE.

sources.title: Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Asian History, The Yuezhi
sources.note: Craig Benjamin’s Oxford reference overview traces a powerful pastoral confederation near Gansu, Xiongnu defeats, westward migration, resettlement in northern Bactria and the later Kushan transformation, while emphasizing the larger Eurasian consequences.

proposedOverrides.summary: A migrating Central Asian confederation that became overlord of Bactria and later contributed the Kushan ruling branch; the atlas’s 200 to 100 BCE geometry is seriously mistimed.

batchIdentityNotes: Exact target yuezhi is indexed circa 200 to 100 BCE and has no tracked card or override before integration.
Its only exact feature is world-bc200: one Polygon, one ring, 26 positions, bbox 72.279723 to 106.044460 east and 30.174730 to 48.408188 north.
Dunhuang and a central Hexi point fall inside that feature; tested Ili, Issyk-Kul, Kashgar, Ferghana, Samarkand, Balkh, Termez, Kabul and Merv points fall outside.
World-bc100 substitutes a vast kushan-empire feature; world-bc1 has no Kushan; world-100 restores a smaller Kushan extent. These are atlas seams, not verified historical changes.
Historical chronology places Xiongnu defeats in 176 and 162 BCE, Yuezhi entry into Bactria around 140 to 130 BCE, five regional chiefs afterward and Kujula’s Kushan consolidation around 30 CE.
The yuezhi and kushan-empire ids remain distinct. The proposed transition links to existing Kushan geometry at the historically supported approximate year rather than sharing the card.
No polygon, burial assemblage, language or genetic identity is projected onto every person inside the atlas shape.
